excerpt: Paano magtanim ng carrots? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant karot (carrot), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant karot. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino farmers usually grow carrots, sown straight on raised beds in the highlands all year and in the lowlands only in the cool months, up to the harvest two to three months later. For highland vegetable growers and lowland farmers trying a cool season crop, with the changes that give straight, smooth roots.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for root crops](/land-preparation/root-crop-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [karot varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/carrot). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [karot nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/carrot-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing.
When to plant karot

In the highlands, such as Benguet, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Nueva Vizcaya and Bukidnon, carrots are sown all year. In low and mid elevations they are sown only in the coolest months, from about the last week of October to February. In hot weather the roots turn pale, woody and misshapen.
What you plant
Seed, about 6 to 8 kg a hectare, sown straight on the bed. Most varieties grown here are short, thick Kuroda types. Growers in the lowlands pick strains that take some heat.
Paano magtanim ng carrots, step by step
The crop is ready about 90 days after sowing.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 21 days before sowing: Plow and harrow until fine
items.text: Plow and harrow several times until the soil is fine and free of clods and stones, because lumps make forked, crooked roots.

items.title: 7 days before sowing: Raise the beds and mix in manure
items.text: Make beds about 20 cm high and 70 to 80 cm wide with 30 cm paths. Work rotted chicken dung and complete fertilizer into the bed about a week before sowing.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Sowing day: Sow in shallow furrows
items.text: Spread the seed evenly along shallow furrows on the bed and cover with fine soil, no more than about 2 cm. Water the beds and lay rice straw over them. Tip: Seedlings take up to two weeks to come up, so keep the bed moist the whole time.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 3: Water every few days
items.text: Carrots need steady moisture in the first month. Water every five to seven days, or more often in dry spells, and keep it even so the roots do not crack or fork.

items.title: Day 14: Move the mulch to the rows
items.text: Once the seedlings are up, lift the straw off the rows and lay it between them to hold moisture and keep weeds down.

items.title: Day 30: Weed and thin
items.text: Pull the weeds and thin the seedlings so the plants stand about 10 cm apart.

items.title: Day 31: Side dress and hill up
items.text: Right after thinning, put the rest of the fertilizer along the rows and cover it as you pull soil up over the shoulders of the roots, which keeps them from turning green.

items.title: Day 40: Scout the beds
items.text: Look for cutworms and mole crickets at the base, aphids and armyworms on the leaves, and leaf blight spots. Remove rotting roots.

items.title: Day 75: Second weeding and hilling up
items.text: About 45 days after the first, weed again and hill up the rows.

items.title: Day 90: Trim, wash and sort
items.text: Cut the tops 5 to 8 cm above the shoulder, wash and air dry the roots, and sort out cracked, forked and broken ones before packing. Bring them out of the sun right away.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 90: Pull the roots
items.text: Two to three months after sowing, once the lower leaves start to yellow and the roots have reached market size, push a spading fork in beside the row to free the soil, then lift the carrots out gently.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for karot
Spacing
Raised beds about 70 to 80 cm wide and 20 cm high with 30 cm paths. Seed sown in shallow furrows on the bed and thinned to about 10 cm between plants.
Water
Watered by sprinkler, hose or furrow every five to seven days, more in dry weather. The first 30 days need the most care. Uneven watering makes roots crack and fork.
Fertilizer

Highland growers rely on rotted chicken dung, about 3 to 5 tons a hectare, with 3 to 5 bags of complete fertilizer worked into the beds a week before sowing. The rest of the nitrogen and potash goes on at about 30 days, after thinning, and is covered during hilling up. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Straw mulch at sowing, moved between rows after the seedlings come up, thinning to about 10 cm at a month, side dressing and hilling up after thinning, and a second weeding and hilling up about 45 days later.
When and how to harvest

Most carrots are pulled two to three months after sowing, when the lower leaves yellow and the roots reach market size. Roots are loosened with a fork, pulled, topped, washed, air dried and sorted, and moved to the shade or packing house quickly.
Common mistakes when planting karot

items: Sowing on cloddy or stony soil, which gives forked and crooked roots.
Fresh, unrotted manure in the beds, which also causes forking.
Skipping the thinning, so the roots stay thin and twisted.
Watering unevenly, dry then soaked, so the roots split.
Sowing in the hot months in the lowlands.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of karot
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Use fresh seed of a variety suited to your elevation and season.
Prepare deep, fine, raised beds and use only well rotted manure.
Test the soil and give potash enough, since carrots need more of it than most leafy crops.
Thin on time and keep the moisture even, with mulch between rows.
Rotate with corn or other crops outside the carrot family to keep root knot nematodes down.
Harvest on time and keep roots cool and shaded after digging.
